### 1. Altitude and Position
The Moon is at an **altitude of 48.3 degrees**. In practical terms, this means it is nearly halfway between the horizon and the zenith (the point directly above your head). It is high enough in the sky to be very prominent and is not "hiding" near the horizon where atmospheric haze might obscure it.

### 2. Azimuth (Direction)
An **azimuth of 271.8 degrees** means the Moon is located almost directly to your **West**. Since the Sun is currently below the horizon (at -10.39 degrees), the western sky is where the light from the setting sun is fading, but the Moon will be standing out clearly against that backdrop.

### 3. Illumination and Phase
At **89.48% illumination**, the Moon is in its "Waxing Gibbous" phase, very close to being a Full Moon. This means it is extremely bright. It is not a thin crescent; it is a large, glowing orb.

### 4. Sky Conditions
You mentioned the sky is **clear** and you are in **nautical twilight**. 
*   **Clear skies** mean there are no clouds to block the view.
*   **Nautical twilight** means the sky is dark enough that the stars are visible, but there is still some ambient light. Because the Moon is nearly full and high in the sky, it will be the brightest object in the heavens, making it impossible to miss.

### Summary
If you look toward the **West** (roughly toward the direction of the ocean/Pacific coast from Santiago), you will see a very large, bright, nearly-full Moon. It will be the dominant feature of the sky.
